title: Infosys in Talks With DOJ Over Investigation Into H-1B Classifications
headline: Infosys in Talks With DOJ Over Investigation Into H-1B Classifications
subheadline: Infosys disclosed in its September-quarter financial statements that the US Department of Justice is investigating how it classified certain H-1B holders in immigration filings, and said it cannot predict the outcome.
body:
• Infosys is in discussions with the US Department of Justice over an ongoing investigation into how the company classified certain H-1B visa holders in immigration documents filed with US authorities.
  • The company disclosed the probe in its financial statements for the quarter and half-year ended September 30, 2026, under the "Government Investigation" section of its legal proceedings, and said it continues its own internal inquiry.
  • Infosys said it cannot predict the outcome or whether the matter will have a material adverse effect on its business — there has been no finding against the company.
  • For H-1B employees: the probe concerns the employer's filings, not individual workers' status, but it underlines why worksite and role details in petitions must match the job actually performed.

Infosys Ltd. is in discussions with the US Department of Justice (DOJ) over an ongoing investigation into how the company classified certain H-1B visa holders in immigration documents submitted to US government authorities, the company disclosed in its financial statements for the quarter and half-year ended September 30, 2026, according to The American Bazaar.

"The Company is engaged in discussions with the DOJ regarding its ongoing investigation and continues its own inquiry regarding the matter."

— Infosys, September-quarter filing

What Is Being Investigated

The disclosure, which appears under the "Government Investigation" section of Infosys's legal proceedings, focuses on the classification of certain H-1B holders in immigration documents — in earlier reporting of the same disclosure, the classification concerned employees working for one of the company's clients, as Gulte reported in September when the disclosure appeared in the June-quarter filing. Classification matters in H-1B filings because the occupation, worksite and duties stated in a petition determine the wage level and the conditions under which the visa was granted; a mismatch between the filing and the actual assignment is a compliance problem even where no fraud is alleged.

Infosys has not disclosed whether the current probe is connected to any earlier matter, and the filing records an investigation and discussions — not a charge, a settlement or a finding.

The 2013 Precedent

The disclosure lands against a long compliance history. In 2013, Infosys paid $34 million to settle a US government probe into alleged immigration violations — at the time a record settlement of its kind. That case resolved allegations that the company had improperly used B-1 business visas for employees performing work in the United States and provided misleading information about the purpose of some visits, alongside violations involving employment eligibility verification records. As part of the settlement, Infosys strengthened its compliance procedures and accepted independent audits of its verification practices; it disputed allegations of widespread visa fraud, and the settlement closed the government's claims without criminal charges.

Why It Matters Now

The renewed scrutiny comes as H-1B enforcement has tightened across the board, with data-driven audits and closer examination of outsourcers' filings. Indian IT services firms are among the largest H-1B sponsors, and Indian nationals receive the largest share of H-1B approvals, so how a sponsor classifies client-site workers is a question with direct consequences for thousands of Indian professionals — even though an employer-side investigation does not, by itself, change any individual employee's immigration status.

For workers, the practical lesson is documentary: the role, worksite and duties in the petition should match the assignment in fact, and any material change — a new client, a new worksite, a substantially different role — is the employer's trigger to assess an amended filing.

What Happens Next

Infosys said it could not predict the outcome of the investigation or determine whether it would have a material adverse effect on its business and operating results. Discussions with the DOJ and the company's own inquiry are continuing. Until the DOJ or the company discloses more, the known facts are narrow: an investigation into classification, a company cooperating and inquiring in parallel, and no conclusion reached.
